donor_findings.title: Engineering serendipity: When does knowledge sharing lead to knowledge production?
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: Managers often try to stimulate innovation by encouraging serendipitous interactions between employees, for example by using office space redesigns, conferences and similar events. Are such interventions effective? ... We conduct a field experiment at a medical research symposium, where we exogenously varied opportunities for face-to-face encounters among 15,817 scientist-pairs ... an effective encounter depends on the degree of common knowledge shared by the individuals.
donor_findings.abstract: Research Summary We investigate how knowledge similarity between two individuals is systematically related to the likelihood that a serendipitous encounter results in knowledge production. We conduct a field experiment at a medical research symposium, where we exogenously varied opportunities for face-to-face encounters among 15,817 scientist-pairs. Our data include direct observations of interaction patterns collected using sociometric badges, and detailed, longitudinal data of the scientists' postsymposium publication records over 6 years. We find that interacting scientists acquire more knowledge and coauthor 1.2 more papers when they share some overlapping interests, but cite each other's work between three and seven times less when they are from the same field. Our findings reveal both collaborative and competitive effects of knowledge similarity on knowledge production outcomes.

donor_findings.title: Serendipity: Chance Encounters in the Marketplace Enhance Consumer Satisfaction
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: This occurs as a result of feelings of serendipity that arise when a marketplace encounter is positive, unexpected, and attributed to some degree of chance ... [the effect is] not effective when the encounter is negative, the encounter occurs deterministically (i.e., planned by marketers to target consumers), and consumers perceive that they have enough knowledge to make their own choices.
donor_findings.abstract: Despite evidence that consumers appreciate freedom of choice, they also enjoy recommendation systems, subscription services, and marketplace encounters that seemingly occur by chance. This article proposes that enjoyment can, in some contexts, be higher than that in contexts involving choice. This occurs as a result of feelings of serendipity that arise when a marketplace encounter is positive, unexpected, and attributed to some degree of chance. A series of studies shows that feelings of serendipity positively influence an array of consumer outcomes, including satisfaction and enjoyment, perceptions of meaningfulness of an experience, likelihood of recommending a company, and likelihood of purchasing additional products from the company. The findings show that strategies based on serendipity are even more effective when consumers perceive that randomness played a role in how an encounter occurred, and not effective when the encounter is negative, the encounter occurs deterministically (i.e., planned by marketers to target consumers), and consumers perceive that they have enough knowledge to make their own choices.

donor_findings.title: Strategic Visibility in Enterprise Social Media: Implications for Network Formation and Boundary Spanning
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: The proliferation of enterprise social media (ESM) and the associated increase in visibility of people, content, and interactions, has resulted in a widespread assumption that unlimited visibility improves boundary spanning ... the distinct ways that ESM visibility—bounded or unbounded—is leveraged strategically to evoke diverse network structures, which in turn have implications for distinct boundary-spanning activities.
donor_findings.abstract: Effective workgroups engage in team boundary spanning, that is, using communication ties as conduits to critical external resources. The proliferation of enterprise social media (ESM) and the associated increase in visibility of people, content, and interactions, has resulted in a widespread assumption that unlimited visibility improves boundary spanning. Consequently, the ESM literature has generally ignored the sentry functions of teams and failed to examine the possible strategic nature of visibility choices by ESM groups. Using log and content data from 655 ESM-based workgroups at a multinational enterprise, we contribute a deeper understanding of the distinct ways that ESM visibility—bounded or unbounded—is leveraged strategically to evoke diverse network structures, which in turn have implications for distinct boundary-spanning activities.

donor_findings.title: Bridging cultural holes in organizations: The dynamic structure of social networks and organizational vocabularies within and across subunits
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: Within subunit boundaries, members who interact with each other are more likely to develop similar vocabularies over time. Interestingly, between subunits, the more two members share similar organizational vocabularies, the more likely they are to form a tie over time ... Organizational vocabularies, we suggest, may sustain communication patterns across organizational boundaries, thus bridging cultural holes within organizations.
donor_findings.abstract: The mechanisms by which social networks and organizational vocabularies combine jointly to affect communication patterns across organizational boundaries remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we examine the mutually constitutive relation between the network ties through which organizational members communicate with each other and the vocabularies that they use to describe their organization. We suggest that the dynamic structure of social networks and organizational vocabularies is contingent on the formal design of organizational subunits. Within subunit boundaries, members who interact with each other are more likely to develop similar vocabularies over time. Interestingly, between subunits, the more two members share similar organizational vocabularies, the more likely they are to form a tie over time. We find empirical evidence for these arguments in a longitudinal study conducted among the managers of a multiunit organization.

donor_findings.title: Team knowledge and coordination in geographically distributed software development
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: geographic distance has a negative effect on coordination, but is mitigated by shared knowledge of the team and presence awareness; and shared task knowledge is more important for coordination among collocated members.
donor_findings.abstract: Coordination is important in software development because it leads to benefits such as cost savings, shorter development cycles, and better-integrated products. Team cognition research suggests that members coordinate through team knowledge, but this perspective has only been investigated in real-time collocated tasks and we know little about which types of team knowledge best help coordination in the most geographically distributed software work. In this field study, we investigate the coordination needs of software teams, how team knowledge affects coordination, and how this effect is influenced by geographic dispersion. Our findings show that software teams have three distinct types of coordination needs—technical, temporal, and process—and that these needs vary with the members' role; geographic distance has a negative effect on coordination, but is mitigated by shared knowledge of the team and presence awareness; and shared task knowledge is more important for coordination among collocated members.

donor_findings.title: Sharing meaning across occupational communities: The transformation of understanding on a production floor
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: the communities' knowledge-sharing difficulties are rooted in differences in their language, the locus of their practice, and their conceptualization of the product. When communication problems arise, if members of these communities provide solutions which invoke the differences in the work contexts and create common ground between the communities, they can transform the understandings of others.
donor_findings.abstract: This paper suggests that knowledge is shared in organizations through the transformation of occupational communities' situated understandings of their work. In this paper, I link the misunderstandings between engineers, technicians, and assemblers on a production floor to their work contexts, and demonstrate how members of these communities overcome such problems by cocreating common ground that transforms their understanding of the product and the production process. In particular, I find that the communities' knowledge-sharing difficulties are rooted in differences in their language, the locus of their practice, and their conceptualization of the product.

donor_findings.title: Integrating distributed work: Comparing task design, communication, and tacit coordination mechanisms
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: we outline a distinctive set of coordination mechanisms that rely on tacit coordination—and theoretically articulate and empirically show that tacit coordination mechanisms are distinct from the well-known duo of coordination strategies: building communication channels or modularizing processes to minimize the need for communication.
donor_findings.abstract: We investigate coordination strategies in integrating distributed work. In the context of Business Process Offshoring (BPO), we analyze survey data from 126 offshored processes to understand both the sources of difficulty in integrating distributed work as well as how organizations overcome these difficulties. We find that interdependence between offshored and onshore processes can lower offshored process performance, and investing in coordination mechanisms can ameliorate the performance impact of interdependence. In particular, we outline a distinctive set of coordination mechanisms that rely on tacit coordination—and theoretically articulate and empirically show that tacit coordination mechanisms are distinct from the well-known duo of coordination strategies: building communication channels or modularizing processes to minimize the need for communication.

donor_findings.title: Boundary spanners' identification, intergroup contact, and effective intergroup relations
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: We examined the relationship between group boundary spanners' work group identification and effective (i.e., harmonious and productive) intergroup relations in 53 work groups in five health care organizations. The data suggest this relationship was moderated by boundary spanners' levels of organizational identification, thus supporting a dual identity model.
donor_findings.abstract: We examined the relationship between group boundary spanners' work group identification and effective (i.e., harmonious and productive) intergroup relations in 53 work groups in five health care organizations. The data suggest this relationship was moderated by boundary spanners' levels of organizational identification, thus supporting a dual identity model. Limited support was found for the moderating effect of intergroup contact. Finally, if boundary spanners displayed frequent intergroup contact and identified highly with their organization, group identification was most strongly related to effective intergroup relations.

donor_findings.title: Work Un(Interrupted): How Non-territorial Space Shapes Worker Control over Social Interaction
donor_findings.relevant_snippet: the old territorial space rendered workers constantly accessible to others, the new non-territorial space altered information about workers' location and availability preferences ... physical spaces certainly structure opportunities for social interaction, [and] they also structure the strategies that individuals can use to actively manage social interaction.
donor_findings.abstract: Organizational research has long emphasized the importance of physical space in structuring opportunities for social interaction among workers. Using 14 months of field research during an office redesign at a large team-based sales company, I find that the adoption of non-territorial space—a change from assigned cubicles to an unassigned mix of spaces—substantially increased worker control over social interaction. Whereas the old territorial space rendered workers constantly accessible to others, the new non-territorial space altered information about workers' location and availability preferences, enabling new strategies for hiding in the space and signaling availability to others through workspace selection. This led to greater reliance on virtual or asynchronous communication technologies, and less unwanted interruption in the new non-territorial space.

theory_elements.x: Physical co-location of organizational members (shared physical presence of the workforce)
theory_elements.y: Volume of work-related contact (frequency and strength of contacts, aggregated across all tie types)
theory_elements.relation_form: Positive linear and uniform: greater co-location yields more interaction opportunities, which yield more frequent, stronger ties, with the effect holding equally for every tie type.
theory_elements.mechanism: Co-location raises the number of spontaneous interaction opportunities (members encounter one another while working); more opportunities raise communication frequency, and frequency sustains tie strength. Removing co-location reduces opportunities, hence frequency, hence tie strength across the board.
theory_elements.assumption: The amount of interaction (opportunity/frequency) is the mediator of the proximity effect, and proximity operates on how MUCH interaction occurs rather than on WHICH ties it flows through.
theory_elements.boundary_conditions: Stated to apply to the whole workforce; the direct application implies that total interaction volume should fall once co-location is removed.

candidates.borrowed_or_modified_construct: (none — this is the null-hypothesis baseline, applying the anchor theory's original construct as-is, with no modification)
candidates.why_existing_insufficient: (none — this is the null-hypothesis baseline, applying the anchor theory's original construct as-is; whether it is sufficient for this phenomenon is exactly what the pairwise tournament tests)
candidates.explanation_of_phenomenon: Applied directly, the anchor theory predicts that removing co-location reduces interaction opportunities for the entire workforce, so all work-related contacts — within-function and cross-function alike — should decline, and total logged interaction should fall. The phenomenon matches only in part: cross-functional contacts collapsed, but within-function contacts were preserved or increased and total logged hours and meeting time were unchanged. The baseline therefore predicts a uniform volume decline that the phenomenon does not show, and it contains no principle by which the effect could become boundary-selective.
candidates.mutual_exclusivity_note: If the baseline is correct — proximity governs the AMOUNT of interaction and all ties therefore rise and fall together with opportunity — then the four alternatives are ruled out, because each posits a compositional force (budget reallocation, frame deficit, encounter generation, or identity salience) that operates even when total interaction volume is held constant, which the volume-only baseline does not admit.

virtue_scores.graph_based_rationale: This candidate sits at the root of the candidate-evidence graph: it is the only one that routes the proximity effect entirely through the volume of interaction, and each alternative is defined by denying that route (C2 reallocates a fixed volume; C4 substitutes one channel for another; C3 and C5 make the effect conditional on frame or identity). It therefore inherits the anchor literature's high parsimony (a single mediator) and coherence, but it contradicts the phenomenon card's most diagnostic datum — the conserved logged hours and meeting time — and cannot support any edge from X to the boundary-selective Y, which is why its precision is lowest. Its consilience is moderate: it unifies the general propinquity findings but nothing else in the graph.

candidates.candidate_name: Conserved Interaction Budget: Discretionary Ties Decay as Effort Reallocates to Role-Anchored Ties

theory_elements.x: Withdrawal of the ambient co-present cues that had tacitly signalled an existing tie's ongoing availability (loss of co-location)
theory_elements.y: Composition of work-related contact: the allocation of a bounded tie-maintenance effort across boundary-crossing versus boundary-contained ties
theory_elements.relation_form: Reallocation under a conserved total (zero-sum reshuffle): total maintenance effort is conserved while its distribution across tie types shifts toward within-unit ties.
theory_elements.mechanism: Actors hold a finite capacity for tie maintenance, mirrored in the conserved logged hours and meeting time. Ties whose maintenance is mandated by the formal role — principally within-unit workflow ties — elicit scheduled contact regardless of physical setting, because the work itself forces the interaction. Ties not mandated by the role — principally cross-unit ties — were sustained largely by ambient, near-zero-cost co-presence cues (seeing someone, passing them, incidental check-ins). When co-location is withdrawn the ambient prompt disappears, and the now-unprompted cross-unit tie must compete for the actor's bounded maintenance effort against role-mandated ties. Actors triage: they let the discretionary cross-boundary ties lapse and reinvest the freed effort within their own unit, leaving interaction volume constant but its composition shifted.
theory_elements.assumption: Tie maintenance is effort-limited and actors allocate that effort preferentially to ties embedded in their formal role; maintenance of cross-boundary ties depended on an ambient prompt rather than on the tie's recognized value.
theory_elements.boundary_conditions: Holds where functional units are the containers of formal roles and where total working hours and meeting time are administratively fixed, so the maintenance budget cannot expand.

candidates.borrowed_or_modified_construct: Kleinbaum's (2018) 'tie decay choices' — the anchor literature's own competing mechanism, stated explicitly against its dominant premise ('most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties'); Kleinbaum shows network change is driven by actors' tie-decay choices conditional on opportunity, not by opportunity alone.
candidates.why_existing_insufficient: The anchor theory's dominant mechanism statements route proximity through a VOLUME mediator — Reagans (2011) via 'communicated more frequently' and Roche et al. (2024) via 'social interactions' and contact frequency. A volume mediator predicts that withdrawing proximity shrinks interaction overall, and so cannot generate a pattern in which total logged hours and meeting time are unchanged while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses. Kleinbaum (2018) names the choice premise but does not theorize how a co-location shock produces a boundary-selective reallocation.
candidates.explanation_of_phenomenon: The co-location shock does not reduce the organization's total interaction capacity — as the unchanged logged hours and meeting time confirm — it removes the low-cost prompt that had kept discretionary cross-boundary ties alive. Once that prompt is gone, cross-boundary ties (not backed by workflow) lose the budget competition to within-unit ties (backed by workflow), so they collapse; within-unit ties are maintained by the work process itself and absorb the redistributed effort, so they hold or rise; and because the budget is conserved, the totals do not move. The decay is boundary-selective precisely because the role boundary is the line between mandated and discretionary ties.
candidates.mutual_exclusivity_note: This candidate locates the cause in deliberate effort allocation, not in a capability deficit. If it holds it rules out C3 (common ground), C4 (encounters) and C5 (identity): those explain collapse through something actors LACK (a shared frame, a generating encounter, a superordinate identity), whereas this candidate says the ties collapse because actors actively stop spending effort on them, and it rules out the baseline by denying that interaction volume is the mediator — proximity's loss reallocates a fixed volume rather than shrinking it.

virtue_scores.graph_based_rationale: This candidate draws its mechanism from the anchor theory's own competing branch (Kleinbaum, 2018) and therefore needs no external vocabulary, keeping parsimony high while explaining more than the baseline. In the candidate-evidence graph it forms an 'explains' edge to three of the phenomenon card's four features — conserved totals, cross-boundary collapse, within-boundary preservation/increase — and a further edge to the literature's unresolved 'opportunity vs. choice' tension, which no other candidate touches. Its only weakness in the graph is lower consilience than C3: it is silent on the interpretive content of what is being maintained, so it cannot absorb the vocabulary/common-ground evidence that C3 can.

candidates.candidate_name: Common-Ground Deficit: Boundary-Crossing Ties Disperse When Their Frame-Generating Setting Is Withdrawn

theory_elements.x: Availability of a co-present, mutually accessible setting that supplies a common frame (shared vocabulary, referent, or material context) to otherwise-unframed dyads
theory_elements.y: Composition of work-related contact across versus within formal subunit boundaries
theory_elements.relation_form: Interaction/conditional: the effect of withdrawing co-location on a tie depends on whether the dyad already shares a frame; frame-poor (cross-boundary) ties are strongly reduced, frame-rich (within-boundary) ties are unaffected.
theory_elements.mechanism: Coordination requires common ground. Members of the same functional unit already share a vocabulary, task frame and locus of practice, and can therefore coordinate through tacit, low-bandwidth signals that need no physical setting; their ties are self-sustaining. Members of different units do not share these frames, and historically built common ground by cocreating it around a co-present material setting. Co-location thus functioned as the common-ground generator for cross-boundary dyads. Withdrawing it removes the setting in which cross-boundary common ground was produced and maintained, so cross-boundary ties — which cannot run on tacit signals alone — disperse; within-boundary ties continue because their common ground never depended on the setting.
theory_elements.assumption: Ongoing coordination requires shared interpretive frames; within-unit actors possess them a priori, while cross-unit actors must generate them and can only generate them in co-present contexts.
theory_elements.boundary_conditions: Holds where formal subunit boundaries coincide with occupational/functional vocabularies, so that the frame gap aligns with the boundary.

candidates.borrowed_or_modified_construct: Tasselli, Zappa & Lomi's (2020) organizational-vocabulary account of cultural holes ('within subunit boundaries, members who interact with each other are more likely to develop similar vocabularies over time ... between subunits, the more two members share similar organizational vocabularies, the more likely they are to form a tie'; 'organizational vocabularies ... may sustain communication patterns across organizational boundaries'), combined with Espinosa et al.'s (2007) finding that geographic distance's negative effect on coordination is 'mitigated by shared knowledge of the team and presence awareness', Bechky's (2003) demonstration that occupational communities bridge their differences by cocreating common ground around material work settings, and Srikanth & Puranam's (2011) tacit-coordination mechanisms in distributed work.
candidates.why_existing_insufficient: The anchor theory's proximity mechanism (Reagans, 2011; Roche et al., 2024) routes the effect through the amount/opportunity of interaction and never conditions it on whether a dyad already shares an interpretive frame, so it cannot generate a boundary-conditional prediction. The common-ground/vocabulary tradition (Tasselli et al., 2020; Bechky, 2003) treats shared frames as a slow dyadic or team property and never ties the SUPPLY of common ground to a physical setting, so it cannot explain how a single co-location shock re-opens the cultural hole between subunits.
candidates.explanation_of_phenomenon: Functional groups are also interpretive communities: an engineer and a marketer at the same firm share neither vocabulary nor task frame (Bechky, 2003). When the workforce is co-located, the shared physical setting lets them build and continuously repair common ground cheaply, and it is this common ground that carries their tie (Tasselli et al., 2020). Remove co-location and the common-ground generator is gone; the cross-functional tie has no frame left to run on and collapses. Within a function the frame is already in place, so the tie survives on digital signals alone and absorbs residual capacity — hence within-function ties hold or rise while total logged time is conserved (Espinosa et al., 2007).
candidates.mutual_exclusivity_note: This candidate grounds the collapse in an interpretive capability gap, not in effort allocation, encounter generation or identity. If it holds it rules out C2, because the ties would then collapse whether or not actors chose to spend effort on them; it rules out C4, because a frame deficit would persist even if unplanned encounters were somehow preserved; and it rules out C5, because the operative deficit is cognitive-linguistic rather than categorical-psychological.

virtue_scores.graph_based_rationale: This candidate has the highest consilience in the set: an 'explains' edge to the cross-boundary collapse, an 'analogy' edge to the whole organizational-vocabulary and team-knowledge literature (Tasselli et al., 2020; Espinosa et al., 2007; Bechky, 2003), and it subsumes C4's encounter observation, since a cocreated frame is precisely what an effective encounter produces (Lane et al., 2021). Its cost is parsimony — it requires a frame-generation step plus an absorption clause for the conserved totals — which is why it loses head-to-head to C4 on parsimony and tot-precision and to C2 on the directness of the conserved-budget argument, even though it beats both on breadth.

candidates.candidate_name: Unplanned-Encounter Generator: Remote Work Destroys the Channel That Carried Cross-Boundary Ties

theory_elements.x: Arrival rate of unplanned, chance-based co-present encounters between members of different groups
theory_elements.y: Count of cross-boundary versus within-boundary work-related contacts
theory_elements.relation_form: Channel-substitution: cross-boundary contacts are proportional to the unplanned-encounter arrival rate (destroyed by remote work), while within-boundary contacts are sustained by the planned-interaction rate (set by the work process and preserved).
theory_elements.mechanism: Co-location is a random-match generator: physical proximity produces unplanned encounters between people who would not have sought each other out. Cross-boundary ties are chronically under-supplied by deliberate search (the anchor literature finds proximity matters most where ex-ante search costs are high), so they are seeded and repeatedly re-affirmed almost entirely by these encounters. Full remote work eliminates the generator, leaving planned interaction as the only surviving channel. Planned interaction is aimed at one's own role-based unit, because that is what the work process schedules. The surviving volume is therefore conserved (meetings still occur, hours are still logged) but is funneled within unit boundaries; the unplanned channel that previously carried the boundary-crossing contacts has no remote substitute.
theory_elements.assumption: Cross-boundary contact value depends on unplanned discovery that planned search cannot substitute, and the planned-interaction channel is directed at role-mandated within-unit partners.
theory_elements.boundary_conditions: Holds where cross-boundary ties are weak, discovery-based or non-mandated rather than embedded in a workflow that forces the interaction.

candidates.disanalogy_note: The serendipity literature does not transfer cleanly. (1) Unit and valence: Lane et al. (2021) and Kim et al. (2021) theorize serendipity as an individual-level discovery that is positively valenced (knowledge production; consumer enjoyment), whereas what is needed here is a neutral, population-level tie-maintenance process — a chance encounter that merely reaffirms or lapses an existing weak tie, carrying no positive affect. (2) A direct inversion is required: Kim et al. (2021) find the serendipity effect disappears when an encounter is seen as PLANNED, but in this setting the planned channel is precisely the one that survives remote work — so what the source literature treats as serendipity's antithesis becomes, here, the residual structure. The adaptation trades away the source literature's affect-based predictions (satisfaction, meaningfulness) in order to retain only its structural claim — that unplanned co-present encounters constitute a distinct, non-substitutable channel — which is what generates the compositional prediction.
candidates.borrowed_or_modified_construct: The serendipitous/accidental-encounter mechanism of Lane et al. (2021: face-to-face encounters as an intentionally engineered generator of knowledge production, exogenously varied via 'opportunities for face-to-face encounters') and Kim et al. (2021: encounters that are positive, unexpected and chance-attributed operate through a channel distinct from planned/choice-driven encounters), with the 'physical space(s) structure opportunities for social interaction' premise from Gonsalves (2023).
candidates.why_existing_insufficient: The anchor theory explains cross-boundary ties through the general opportunity/frequency mechanism, so it cannot distinguish a channel that carries cross-boundary ties (unplanned co-present encounters) from a channel that does not (planned meetings), and therefore cannot explain why the totals are conserved. The serendipity literature is confined to dyadic discovery outcomes and never models the composition of an organization-wide contact network, so it cannot explain why only the cross-boundary subset of ties would be lost.
candidates.explanation_of_phenomenon: The remote shift does not change the amount of scheduled work interaction — hence the unchanged totals — it eliminates the ambient encounter process that had been the sole realistic source of contacts outside one's own function. Cross-functional contacts were almost entirely carried by that process, so they collapse; same-function contacts are carried by the work process and are scheduled regardless of setting, so they persist. The result is a fixed interaction volume whose composition has been stripped of everything that depended on accidental co-presence.
candidates.mutual_exclusivity_note: This candidate makes the collapse a matter of a destroyed generating process rather than a deficit in actors' frames (C3), effort (C2) or identities (C5). If it holds it rules out C3 and C5, because those would predict that cross-boundary ties can be restored by supplying a frame or an identity without restoring encounters; it rules out C2, because the ties were never dropped by choice — the process that produced them simply ceased to operate; and it rules out the baseline, because it denies that proximity affects interaction volume at all, asserting that it affects only the channel through which boundary-crossing contact flows.

virtue_scores.graph_based_rationale: This candidate forms a clean two-node subgraph: one mechanism (a destroyed unplanned-encounter channel) explains both the cross-boundary collapse and the conserved totals without a separate absorption assumption, keeping parsimony at 4 despite the borrowed vocabulary. It has a strong 'explains' edge to the anchor literature's own finding that proximity seeds NEW cross-cutting ties (Catalini, 2018; Chai & Freeman, 2019). Its precision is capped at 4 because in the phenomenon graph it has no edge to the fate of ESTABLISHED cross-boundary ties, which do not require a fresh encounter to persist; C2 does cover that node. Its disanalogy cost (inverting Kim et al.'s 2021 positive-valence framing) is recorded rather than scored down, per the design assumption that a rough borrowing is not by itself a defect.

candidates.candidate_name: Category Re-Salience: Losing Co-Presence Revives Functional Group Identity and Contracts Cross-Boundary Contact

theory_elements.x: Salience of an inclusive superordinate (organization-level) category relative to subgroup (functional) categories
theory_elements.y: Composition of work-related contact across versus within functional boundaries
theory_elements.relation_form: Interaction: the effect of withdrawing co-location on cross-boundary contacts is moderated by the salience of the superordinate versus subgroup category.
theory_elements.mechanism: Shared physical space continuously enacts a superordinate identity — the same floor, same building, the same visible collective — which blurs subunit categories and renders cross-subunit interaction category-neutral. Within-subunit ties are driven by subgroup identification and are unaffected or strengthened as the superordinate frame recedes, because subgroup identity becomes relatively more salient. Remote work strips the physical carriers of the superordinate category (shared space, symbols, spontaneous collective presence), so functional subcategories re-emerge as the operative categories and members confine contact to their own group.
theory_elements.assumption: Group boundaries are psychologically constructed and their behavioral permeability depends on situational cues, including physical co-presence.
theory_elements.boundary_conditions: Holds where functional subunits are identity-relevant categories rather than purely administrative labels.

candidates.borrowed_or_modified_construct: Richter et al.'s (2006) dual-identity model of intergroup relations — group identification, organizational identification and intergroup contact jointly predicting effective ('harmonious and productive') intergroup relations across 53 work groups — the intergroup-relations tradition's account of when members of distinct groups interact across group boundaries.
candidates.why_existing_insufficient: The anchor theory is a structural/opportunity account with no psychological category mechanism: it explains why people in proximity interact more, not why the boundary between functional groups would become behaviorally decisive. The intergroup-relations tradition (Richter et al., 2006) explains the QUALITY of intergroup relations given contact but treats the supply of contact as exogenous and never ties it to a physical setting; neither literature explains why a single co-location shock acts differentially on cross- versus within-boundary ties.

[HARD LANGUAGE REQUIREMENT] For this task, all final structured-output field content (not just your thinking) must be written in English — do not switch to any other language for the substantive content, even if it would otherwise feel natural to you. Established theory names, author citations, and technical terms may keep their standard form. This requirement takes priority over any default habit implied elsewhere in the task instructions.

---

You are a senior management/organization theory theorist, skilled at starting from a well-specified
research question and constructing a genuinely new theoretical explanation — not simply reapplying an
off-the-shelf framework, but being able to state clearly "which existing construct was borrowed/modified,
why the existing construct falls short, and exactly what is new about the mechanism," with every such
claim traceable to real literature rather than a vague impression drawn from training knowledge. You are
now deployed as the execution agent for ATBA's (Abductive Theory-Building Agent) Step 4, "Abductive
Reasoning & Theory Construction."

## Input

You will receive:
- **The phenomenon card** (Step 1's output): `actor`/`observed_behavior`/`field_constraints`/
  `apparent_motive`/`observable_outcome`.
- **The research question** (Step 3's output): the specific RQ text, the candidate theoretical direction
  it is anchored to, which type it is (theoretical-void / mechanism-gap / problematization), and the
  rationale supporting it. **If the type is mechanism-gap, you'll also be told the nature of the gap**
  (see "How the gap's nature shapes candidate generation" below).
- **A deep-dive search on the anchor theory** (Step 3's output, `anchor_theory_grounding`): this theory's
  currently known boundary conditions, internal tensions/gaps, and key literature — **this is background
  material, not your search target**. Step 3 has already thoroughly mapped this theory itself; your own
  search budget goes elsewhere (see the next item).
- **The literature Step 3 actually retrieved** (with abstracts, grouped by examined direction, not
  limited to the one direction that ultimately produced the research question) — also background material.
- If applicable, **the user's own guess** (the causal explanation Step 1's causal-presupposition check
  identified as already implicit in the user's input): for reference during candidate generation only,
  not something already adopted — you're free to generate a different candidate, or to judge that it
  actually holds up.
- If this is a **revision round** (round_number > 1): you'll additionally receive the prior round's
  mechanism-grounding search result and candidate set, the core-mechanism flaw Step 5's interrogation
  found, and **exactly which candidate and which field it named** — see "Special requirements for
  revision rounds" below.

## Task: five sub-steps, completed in sequence within one run

**The focus of this step is the theoretical contribution itself** — turning the research question into
a defensible candidate explanation, spelling out its theoretical elements, and producing a relative
ranking; you do not judge novelty or make a Lakatos-style hard-core/protective-belt determination. Whether
a candidate overlaps with existing literature, or whether its refinement counts as "progressive," is left
to Step 5's interrogation.

0. **Mechanism-sourcing search** (must be done before candidate generation) — **this is the most
   substantially changed step this round; read carefully**:

   Your task is **not** to keep digging into the anchor theory (Step 3 has already done that, see
   `anchor_theory_grounding` above). What abduction should really be looking for is a mechanism that
   "steps outside" the anchor theory — into some other existing theory/mechanism tradition that already
   has a causal logic that can explain this gap. A theory failing to explain some part of a phenomenon
   does not mean the answer lies within that same theory; it's more likely that some other tradition
   already has a causal logic that could be borrowed (or adapted) — it just hasn't been connected to
   this phenomenon before.

   Concretely, this is two steps:
   1. **First distill one sentence of abstract mechanism-pattern description** (`abstract_mechanism_
      pattern`) — naming no theory, no discipline, just describing "what kind of causal logic would be
      needed to explain this gap." Distill it from `anchor_theory_grounding.internal_tensions_or_gaps`
      (the tensions/blind spots this theory's own literature hasn't resolved) — don't invent it out of
      thin air.
      - Bad examples (name a theory, disqualified): "resource dependence theory," "institutional theory's
        mimetic isomorphism"
      - Good examples (describe only the causal structure): "resource-acquisition pressure driving
        strategic escalation," "the gap between expectation and reality driving a behavioral reversal"
   2. **Search using this abstract description** (see "Retrieval skill" below for how) — **do not put
      the anchor theory's name or its discipline's keywords into the search query**. The query should
      track the causal structure of this abstract description, so it can hit literature that is
      structurally similar but from a completely unrelated domain (this is deliberate: if the query
      carries the theory's name, what it finds will naturally only be literature from the same
      theoretical tradition — that's not "stepping outside" at all).

   Compile the result into `mechanism_grounding`: `donor_findings` collects the literature you found that
   might offer a borrowable mechanism. **`donor_findings` may be empty** — if an exhaustive search
   genuinely turns up no suitable external mechanism, report that honestly; a candidate may then take the
   `within_tradition` route (its mechanism comes from `anchor_theory_grounding` rather than here), but
   its `borrowed_or_modified_construct` must honestly say "this did not step outside; it's a mechanism
   dug out from within the same tradition" — don't pretend to have found something that wasn't found.

1. **Candidate generation**: generate **3-5 mutually exclusive** candidate theoretical explanations —
   "mutually exclusive" means each candidate, if true, rules out the others being true; it is not "each
   explains part of the phenomenon" (that's complementary, not the candidate set required here).

   **One candidate must be a null-hypothesis baseline** (`is_baseline=True`): this candidate is simply
   "the anchor theory applied as-is, with no borrowing or modification." Its `mechanism_borrowing_pattern`
   must be `within_tradition`, `disanalogy_note` stays empty, and `borrowed_or_modified_construct`/
   `why_existing_insufficient` may just say "(none — this is the null-hypothesis baseline, directly
   reusing the anchor theory's existing constructs, with no modification)" without pointing to newly
   retrieved literature. Whether the other candidates are genuinely worth adopting has to be established
   by comparing them against this baseline — don't assume every newly generated candidate automatically
   beats "changing nothing." This candidate still fully participates in the pairwise tournament below,
   scored and compared by the same standards as everyone else — no special treatment.

   Each candidate must explicitly classify its own mechanism source (`mechanism_borrowing_pattern`) —
   **don't default to cross-tradition borrowing just to "look more creative."** Based on what was
   actually found in your search, fill in whichever pattern the candidate's mechanism actually came from:
   - `within_tradition`: the mechanism comes from `anchor_theory_grounding` — a competing mechanism dug
     out from within the anchor theory's own literature that was previously assumed but never
     systematically examined (not simply "filling a void" — it points to a previously implicit
     explanatory path worth examining on its own).
   - `adjacent_bridging`: connects a related but non-anchor theoretical tradition — one that is rarely
     discussed alongside the anchor theory, but genuinely offers a complementary lens.
   - `cross_tradition_borrowing`: borrows an external theoretical vocabulary/mechanism with no
     relationship to the anchor theory at all — **this case requires an additional `disanalogy_note`**,
     explaining where this borrowed mechanism **doesn't fit** in the new setting and what adaptations/
     trade-offs were made to make it fit. Don't present only the "successful borrowing" part — real
     theoretical breakthroughs often happen exactly at this "doesn't transfer cleanly" spot, not in the
     borrowing itself (if you feel this borrowing is seamless and needs no adjustment at all, you likely
     haven't examined the disanalogy carefully — go back and think again).

   Each candidate must state: which specific paper(s) were borrowed from or modified (`cross_tradition_
   borrowing`/`adjacent_bridging` should point to `mechanism_grounding.donor_findings`; `within_tradition`
   should point to `anchor_theory_grounding.key_findings` — **you may not point to a construct that
   simply wasn't retrieved, nor fill in details missing from the search results using a vague impression
   from training knowledge**), and why this existing construct is insufficient to cover the research
   question Step 3 located (not just "no one has studied this" — be specific at the mechanism/assumption
   level).

   **How the gap's nature shapes candidate generation** (applies only when Step 3's type is
   mechanism-gap):
   - If the gap's nature is `uncharted` (existing theory genuinely hasn't studied this): candidate
     generation's task is to **fill the void** — the borrowed (or dug-out) mechanism should be able to
     cover this unexplored territory.
   - If the gap's nature is `anomalous_reversal` (the existing theory's core logic, applied directly,
     would predict the opposite result): candidate generation's task is not to sidestep this core logic
     and start fresh to "fill a void," but to **explain how the candidate theory revises/extends this
     core logic** so that it can accommodate both the original prediction and this phenomenon's observed
     reversal — the candidate's `why_existing_insufficient` must directly name what this core logic is,
     what it originally predicts, and why it reverses here; it may not dodge this contradiction.

   **The candidate set's mechanism-borrowing patterns must show genuine breadth**: across all candidates
   (baseline included), `mechanism_borrowing_pattern` must cover at least 2 distinct values with 3-4
   candidates, and all 3 values with 5 candidates — the baseline is always `within_tradition`, so at least
   one of the remaining candidates must be `adjacent_bridging` or `cross_tradition_borrowing`; don't let
   every candidate pile onto `within_tradition`. If several candidates are all `within_tradition`, they're
   probably just different phrasings of the same idea, not genuinely different explanatory directions.

2. **Relationship-graph construction (internal reasoning, not a separate output)**: in your own
   reasoning process, work through the explain/contradict/analogy relationships between candidates and
   evidence, and between candidates themselves — this is the basis for the next step's pairwise
   tournament, especially the rationale behind each pairwise judgment. This doesn't need to be a separate
   output field, but both `virtue_scores.graph_based_rationale` and each `pairwise_comparisons.rationale`
   must show you've actually done this relationship-mapping work — they cannot be conclusions pulled from
   thin air.

3. **Pairwise tournament** (this round's replacement for "each candidate scores itself in isolation"):
   still score each candidate 1-5 on consilience/coherence/parsimony/precision (`virtue_scores`, for
   reviewers' reference). **These four are not the same kind of judgment**: consilience/coherence/
   parsimony evaluate the logical/aesthetic quality of the explanation itself; precision is the only one
   that evaluates "how closely this explanation's specific prediction matches the specific details of the
   phenomenon/research question" (e.g., whether it's rise-then-fall or fall-then-rise — a specific shape,
   not just a vague "nonlinear relationship"). A candidate can be highly parsimonious and coherent yet
   score low on precision (a vague direction that doesn't match the phenomenon's specific shape) — don't
   inflate precision just because the other three scored high. **The final ranking is no longer something
   you assert directly** — you must produce one `pairwise_comparisons` record for every pair of candidates
   in `candidates` (3 candidates = 3 pairs, 5 candidates = 10 pairs, none may be skipped; the baseline
   candidate participates in the comparisons too), judging which one in each pair is stronger (or, if
   they're genuinely too close to call, mark it `tie` — don't force a pick just to "look decisive"), with
   a rationale. **The ranking will be computed by code from these pairwise judgments**, so the quality of
   your judgments here directly determines whether the ranking is right — don't go through the motions;
   genuinely compare every pair.

4. **Selection**: `selection_rationale` synthesizes the pairwise comparison results, explaining why the
   ultimately selected candidate (the one with the most pairwise wins) holds up, or — if multiple
   candidates are tied on wins — where the tie is and why it's hard to settle decisively.

## Special requirements for revision rounds (applies when round_number > 1)

Step 5's independent interrogation agent found that some candidate's **core mechanism** from the prior
round doesn't hold up (not a minor issue like boundary conditions that can be tightened later), and has
fed the specific flaw back to you — **explicitly naming which candidate and which specific field**
(unless it genuinely can't be pinned to a specific field, in which case it names "the whole candidate").
This round you need to:
- **By default, directly reuse the prior round's `mechanism_grounding` without re-searching** — the
  theoretical landscape doesn't change because of one round of interrogation; only search again, and
  only for that specific gap, if the feedback explicitly points to "a mechanism direction was missed."
- **Locate precisely, and only change the part that was named**: if a specific field was named, **rewrite
  only that one field of that one candidate** — that candidate's other fields, and every candidate that
  wasn't named, must be **kept exactly as-is and copied verbatim into your output**. Don't touch anything
  that wasn't flagged just because you feel like "improving it while you're at it" — this discipline is
  new this round; the previous phrasing "no need to start over" was too vague and easily read as "change
  whatever I feel like changing." If "the whole candidate" was named (the core mechanism as a whole
  doesn't hold up), reconstruct that entire candidate — but every other candidate is still kept as-is.
- **Revise targetedly**: respond directly to this specific flaw — don't just restate the same mechanism
  in different words, and don't paper over the problem while pretending it's solved.
- Still provide a complete `mechanism_grounding` (reusable from the prior round), a complete set of 3-5
  candidates (unrevised ones copied verbatim), and a complete `pairwise_comparisons` — **even if most
  candidates' content is unchanged, re-run the pairwise comparisons from scratch**, because the revised
  candidate's relative strength against the others may have changed; you cannot carry over the prior
  round's ranking.

Call the tool `report_step4_output` to give your final result. Do not output any text outside the tool call.

## Retrieval Skill: How to Use the `search_scopus` and `get_paper_abstract` Tools Well

You have two tools:
- `search_scopus(query, max_results)` — give it a Scopus concept query and it automatically adds the
  UTD24 journal-range restriction and returns real results (a paper list + total hit count). **You must
  decide for yourself what to search, how many rounds to run, and when you have searched enough** — a
  single tool call is not enough. This is the most important part of this skill: search is a process you
  drive by judging results and adjusting, not "generate one query and stop."
- `get_paper_abstract(doi)` — the paper list `search_scopus` returns does not itself carry
  abstracts (a Scopus API limitation); to read a paper's full abstract, look it up by its `doi` (not
  `scopus_id`) with this tool, which internally tries Semantic Scholar then OpenAlex. **Only call it for papers you have decided to cite** (i.e. ones going into the final
  `cited_evidence`) — most search results only serve to judge "is this query on target," and the papers
  you actually end up citing are usually just a few; fetching an abstract for every hit wastes quota.
  Conversely, **before deciding to cite a paper, you must fetch its abstract first** — don't judge
  whether a paper supports/contradicts a conclusion from the title alone; a title rarely reveals which
  specific mechanism the paper actually covers.

### Scopus query syntax

- `TITLE-ABS-KEY()`: searches title, abstract, and keywords together (most common, broadest coverage —
  default to this)
- `TITLE()` / `ABS()` / `KEY()`: title / abstract / keywords only
- `AUTH()`: author name; `PUBYEAR`: publication year; `DOCTYPE()`: document type (ar=article, re=review)
- Boolean operators `AND`/`OR`/`AND NOT`, parentheses for grouping, quotes for phrases, `*` for wildcards
- Write only the concept part — **do not construct the journal-range restriction yourself** (the
  EXACTSRCTITLE-based UTD24 filter is added automatically by the tool)
- If what you're searching for is originally in Chinese, translate it into standard English academic

content.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We investigate how knowledge similarity between two individuals is systematically related to the likelihood that a serendipitous encounter results in knowledge production. We conduct a field experiment at a medical research symposium, where we exogenously varied opportunities for face‐to‐face encounters among 15,817 scientist‐pairs. Our data include direct observations of interaction patterns collected using sociometric badges, and detailed, longitudinal data of the scientists' postsymposium publication records over 6 years. We find that interacting scientists acquire more knowledge and coauthor 1.2 more papers when they share some overlapping interests, but cite each other's work between three and seven times less when they are from the same field. Our findings reveal both collaborative and competitive effects of knowledge similarity on knowledge production outcomes. Managerial Summary Managers often try to stimulate innovation by encouraging serendipitous interactions between employees, for example by using office space redesigns, conferences and similar events. Are such interventions effective? This article proposes that an effective encounter depends on the degree of common knowledge shared by the individuals. We find that scientists who attend the same conference are more likely to learn from each other and collaborate effectively when they have some common interests, but may view each other competitively when they work in the same field. Hence, when designing opportunities for face‐to‐face interactions, managers should consider knowledge similarity as a criteria for fostering more productive exchanges.

Effective workgroups engage in team boundary spanning, that is, using communication ties as conduits to critical external resources. The proliferation of enterprise social media (ESM) and the associated increase in visibility of people, content, and interactions, has resulted in a widespread assumption that unlimited visibility improves boundary spanning. Consequently, the ESM literature has generally ignored the sentry functions of teams and failed to examine the possible strategic nature of visibility choices by ESM groups. Using log and content data from 655 ESM-based workgroups at a multinational enterprise, we contribute a deeper understanding of the distinct ways that ESM visibility—bounded or unbounded—is leveraged strategically to evoke diverse network structures, which in turn have implications for distinct boundary-spanning activities. Practically, these findings show that ESM present a unique opportunity for workgroups to simultaneously sustain multiple virtual spaces—with varying levels of visibility—through which they can manage their diverse boundary-spanning goals.

The mechanisms by which social networks and organizational vocabularies combine jointly to affect communication patterns across organizational boundaries remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we examine the mutually constitutive relation between the network ties through which organizational members communicate with each other and the vocabularies that they use to describe their organization. We suggest that the dynamic structure of social networks and organizational vocabularies is contingent on the formal design of organizational subunits. Within subunit boundaries, members who interact with each other are more likely to develop similar vocabularies over time. Interestingly, between subunits, the more two members share similar organizational vocabularies, the more likely they are to form a tie over time. We find empirical evidence for these arguments in a longitudinal study conducted among the managers of a multiunit organization. Organizational vocabularies, we suggest, may sustain communication patterns across organizational boundaries, thus bridging cultural holes within organizations.

Coordination is important in software development because it leads to benefits such as cost savings, shorter development cycles, and better-integrated products. Team cognition research suggests that members coordinate through team knowledge, but this perspective has only been investigated in real-time collocated tasks and we know little about which types of team knowledge best help coordination in the most geographically distributed software work. In this field study, we investigate the coordination needs of software teams, how team knowledge affects coordination, and how this effect is influenced by geographic dispersion. Our findings show that software teams have three distinct types of coordination needs—technical, temporal, and process—and that these needs vary with the members' role; geographic distance has a negative effect on coordination, but is mitigated by shared knowledge of the team and presence awareness; and shared task knowledge is more important for coordination among collocated members. We articulate propositions for future research in this area based on our analysis.

We examined the relationship between group boundary spanners' work group identification and effective (i. E., harmonious and productive) intergroup relations in 53 work groups in five health care organizations. The data suggest this relationship was moderated by boundary spanners' levels of organizational identification, thus supporting a dual identity model. Limited support was found for the moderating effect of intergroup contact. Finally, if boundary spanners displayed frequent intergroup contact and identified highly with their organization, group identification was most strongly related to effective intergroup relations.

Organizational research has long emphasized the importance of physical space in structuring opportunities for social interaction among workers. Using 14 months of field research during an office redesign at a large team-based sales company, I find that the adoption of non-territorial space—a change from assigned cubicles to an unassigned mix of spaces—substantially increased worker control over social interaction. Whereas the old territorial space rendered workers constantly accessible to others, the new non-territorial space altered information about workers’ location and availability preferences, enabling new strategies for hiding in the space and signaling availability to others through workspace selection. This led to greater reliance on virtual or asynchronous communication technologies, and less unwanted interruption in the new non-territorial space. The findings identify how the non-territorial dimension of office space affects worker control over social interaction. They also reveal the social practices through which individuals actively use material and symbolic resources in the physical environment to avoid cognitive and temporal costs of unwanted interruption. The study complements dominant structural accounts with a richer theorization of individual agency—while physical spaces certainly structure opportunities for social interaction, they also structure the strategies that individuals can use to actively manage social interaction.

Abstract We investigate coordination strategies in integrating distributed work. In the context of Business Process Offshoring (BPO), we analyze survey data from 126 offshored processes to understand both the sources of difficulty in integrating distributed work as well as how organizations overcome these difficulties. We find that interdependence between offshored and onshore processes can lower offshored process performance, and investing in coordination mechanisms can ameliorate the performance impact of interdependence. In particular, we outline a distinctive set of coordination mechanisms that rely on tacit coordination—and theoretically articulate and empirically show that tacit coordination mechanisms are distinct from the well‐known duo of coordination strategies: building communication channels or modularizing processes to minimize the need for communication. We discuss implications for the study of coordination in organizations. Copyright © 2010 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

This paper suggests that knowledge is shared in organizations through the transformation of occupational communities' situated understandings of their work. In this paper, I link the misunderstandings between engineers, technicians, and assemblers on a production floor to their work contexts, and demonstrate how members of these communities overcome such problems by cocreating common ground that transforms their understanding of the product and the production process. In particular, I find that the communities' knowledge-sharing difficulties are rooted in differences in their language, the locus of their practice, and their conceptualization of the product. When communication problems arise, if members of these communities provide solutions which invoke the differences in the work contexts and create common ground between the communities, they can transform the understandings of others and generate a richer understanding of the product and the problems they face.

Despite evidence that consumers appreciate freedom of choice, they also enjoy recommendation systems, subscription services, and marketplace encounters that seemingly occur by chance. This article proposes that enjoyment can, in some contexts, be higher than that in contexts involving choice. This occurs as a result of feelings of serendipity that arise when a marketplace encounter is positive, unexpected, and attributed to some degree of chance. A series of studies shows that feelings of serendipity positively influence an array of consumer outcomes, including satisfaction and enjoyment, perceptions of meaningfulness of an experience, likelihood of recommending a company, and likelihood of purchasing additional products from the company. The findings show that strategies based on serendipity are even more effective when consumers perceive that randomness played a role in how an encounter occurred, and not effective when the encounter is negative, the encounter occurs deterministically (i.e., planned by marketers to target consumers), and consumers perceive that they have enough knowledge to make their own choices. Altogether, this research suggests that marketers can influence customer satisfaction by structuring marketplace encounters to appear more serendipitous, as opposed to expected or entirely chosen by the consumer.
